title: The Republic
author: Plato
blurb: The foundational dialogue on justice, the ideal state, and the philosopher-king. The allegory of the cave still frames how we argue about truth and politics.
prompt: Is Plato's 'philosopher-king' a dream worth having, or the first step toward tyranny?

title: Politics
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's survey of constitutions and the claim that humans are 'political animals.' The origin of thinking about the middle class as the stabiliser of states.
prompt: Aristotle thought a large middle class makes states stable. Does that hold up today?

title: The Prince
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
blurb: The unsentimental handbook on power: is it better to be loved or feared? Still the sharpest short read on how politics actually works versus how we wish it did.
prompt: Loved or feared? Where do modern leaders you know land?

title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes
blurb: Life in the state of nature as 'nasty, brutish, and short,' and the social contract that trades liberty for security. The starting gun for modern political theory.
prompt: How much freedom would you trade for security? Hobbes says almost all of it.

title: The Social Contract
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
blurb: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Rousseau's case for popular sovereignty and the general will that shaped every revolution since.
prompt: What is the 'general will' and can a whole society really have one?

title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill
blurb: The clearest defence of free speech and individual liberty ever written, and the 'harm principle' that still anchors every debate about where freedom ends.
prompt: Mill's harm principle: the only reason to limit someone's freedom is harm to others. Too permissive, or exactly right?

title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
author: Edmund Burke
blurb: The founding text of conservatism: a defence of tradition, gradual change, and inherited institutions against revolutionary reason.
prompt: Burke distrusted sweeping change built on abstract principle. Wisdom or excuse for the status quo?

title: The Communist Manifesto
author: Marx & Engels
blurb: The most consequential pamphlet in history. Whether you love or loathe it, its analysis of class and capital is impossible to argue about without reading.
prompt: Which part of Marx's critique of capitalism has aged best, and which worst?

title: Democracy in America
author: Alexis de Tocqueville
blurb: A Frenchman's astonishingly prescient 1830s tour of American democracy, civil society, and the 'tyranny of the majority.'
prompt: Tocqueville feared the 'tyranny of the majority.' Do you see it today?

title: The Road to Serfdom
author: Friedrich Hayek
blurb: The classic warning that central planning, however well-intentioned, tends toward the loss of freedom. The intellectual backbone of modern classical liberalism.
prompt: Does Hayek's warning about central planning apply to modern regulated economies, or only to full socialism?

title: A Theory of Justice
author: John Rawls
blurb: Design a society from behind a 'veil of ignorance,' not knowing who you'll be in it. The most influential work of political philosophy of the 20th century.
prompt: Behind Rawls' veil of ignorance, what society would you actually design?

title: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
author: Robert Nozick
blurb: The great libertarian reply to Rawls: a defence of the minimal state and the primacy of individual rights and property.
prompt: Nozick vs Rawls: minimal state or redistribution? Where do you land and why?

title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
author: Hannah Arendt
blurb: How lonely, atomised masses give rise to total domination. Arendt's anatomy of how democracies die is more relevant every year.
prompt: Arendt linked loneliness and isolation to the rise of totalitarianism. Do you buy the connection?

author: George Orwell
blurb: Not just a novel but a permanent political vocabulary: doublethink, Big Brother, the memory hole. The definitive warning about surveillance and language.
prompt: Which is the more accurate warning for today: Orwell's 1984 or Huxley's Brave New World?

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
blurb: Control through pleasure rather than pain: a society kept docile by comfort, distraction, and engineered happiness.
prompt: Is a society that controls you through pleasure worse than one that controls you through fear?

title: The Gulag Archipelago
author: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
blurb: The monumental first-hand account of the Soviet camp system, and the moral line that 'runs through every human heart.'
prompt: Solzhenitsyn said the line between good and evil runs through every heart. What does that mean for how we judge history's villains?

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
blurb: The private notebook of a Roman emperor practising Stoicism. Timeless on duty, mortality, and keeping your head when the world doesn't.
prompt: What is the single most useful piece of Stoic advice for modern life?

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
blurb: 'God is dead' and what comes after: the will to power, the eternal recurrence, and the challenge to create your own values.
prompt: If Nietzsche is right that we must create our own values, where do you start?

title: Beyond Good and Evil
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
blurb: Nietzsche's assault on conventional morality and the 'herd instinct.' Provocative, aphoristic, and endlessly quotable.
prompt: Is conventional morality just, as Nietzsche claimed, the morality of the herd?

title: Being and Time
author: Martin Heidegger
blurb: Dense but foundational: what does it mean to be? Heidegger reframes existence around time, death, and authenticity.
prompt: What would living 'authentically' actually look like, in Heidegger's sense?

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
author: Albert Camus
blurb: If life is absurd and meaningless, why not end it? Camus' answer is to imagine Sisyphus happy. The essential text on the absurd.
prompt: Camus says we must imagine Sisyphus happy. Is that a real answer to the absurd, or a dodge?

title: Discipline and Punish
author: Michel Foucault
blurb: How modern power stopped punishing bodies and started disciplining minds. The panopticon as a model for the whole society.
prompt: Are we all living in Foucault's panopticon now, watching ourselves?

title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
blurb: The founding text of economics: the invisible hand, the division of labour, and why self-interest can serve the common good.
prompt: Smith is claimed by both the left and the right. Who reads him more accurately?

title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century
author: Thomas Piketty
blurb: The data-driven argument that when returns on capital outpace growth, inequality compounds. The economics book everyone argued about.
prompt: Piketty's r > g: is compounding inequality baked into capitalism, or fixable?
